Abel-meholah
AY-bel-meh-HOH-luh
proper noun
From the Hebrew, meaning “meadow of dancing” or “the dancing field”, from abel, a meadow, and a root for dancing.

Biblical Definition

Abel-meholah was a town in the Jordan valley, within the borders of the Israelite tribes east of the central highlands, remembered for two events far apart in time. The first was in the day of Gideon’s great deliverance. When the LORD set the Midianites every man’s sword against his fellow, the host fled, and the rout ran “to the border of Abelmeholah, unto Tabbath” (Jdg 7:22). Thus the town marked the edge of that famous victory, won not by Israel’s might but by the LORD’s breaking of three hundred pitchers and the cry of His sword. The second and greater association is that Abel-meholah was the home of Elisha the son of Shaphat. When the LORD commissioned the weary Elijah at Horeb, He bade him anoint Elisha to be prophet in his room. Elijah came and found him plowing — “Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was of Abelmeholah” (1Ki 19:16) — with twelve yoke of oxen, and cast his mantle upon him. Elisha rose, slew his oxen, gave the flesh to the people, and followed Elijah to be his minister (1Ki 19:19–21). The town was also named in Solomon’s provision districts (1Ki 4:12). Abel-meholah, the meadow of dancing, thus stands as the threshing-floor of a prophet’s call — the place where a plowman left the field to take up the mantle of the man of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A town in the Jordan valley, the home of the prophet Elisha and a marker on the route of Gideon’s rout of Midian.

expand to see more

ABEL-MEHOLAH, a town in the Jordan valley, the birthplace of the prophet Elisha.

The fleeing Midianites were chased to its border in Gideon’s victory (Jdg 7:22).

Elijah found Elisha plowing there and cast his mantle on him (1Ki 19:16).

Elisha left his oxen and followed Elijah to be his minister (1Ki 19:21).

It was named among Solomon’s twelve provision districts (1Ki 4:12).

Key Scripture

1Ki 19:16 — "And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room."

1Ki 19:19 — "So he departed thence, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him."

Jdg 7:22 — "And the three hundred blew the trumpets, and the LORD set every man's sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host: and the host fled to Bethshittah in Zererath, and to the border of Abelmeholah, unto Tabbath."

1Ki 4:12 — "Baana the son of Ahilud; to him pertained Taanach and Megiddo, and all Bethshean, which is by Zartanah beneath Jezreel, from Bethshean to Abelmeholah, even unto the place that is beyond Jokneam:"

Modern Corruption

The lesson to recover is the sovereign call of God, who takes a plowman from his field to be a prophet, and whose victories are His own.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Abel-meholah is the sovereignty of God in calling His servants. Elisha was at his honest labor, plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, when the mantle fell upon him. He sought no office; God sought him. The call to ministry is not seized but bestowed, and the man whom God calls leaves his oxen behind.

The town’s earlier memory enforces the same truth. Gideon’s three hundred won no battle by their pitchers and trumpets; the LORD set the swords of Midian against themselves, and the rout ran past Abel-meholah. Whether in routing armies or in raising prophets, the meadow of dancing testifies that the work is God’s, and the glory His alone.

Hebrew Roots

The name joins abel, a meadow, with a word for dancing, hence “meadow of dancing.”

expand to see more

Abel-meholah — “meadow of dancing” or “the dancing field.”

Abel means a grassy meadow, common in valley place-names.

The latter element comes from a root for dance or whirling.

It lay in the fertile Jordan valley fit for plowing and pasture.

Its sense suits the broad, green plain where Elisha drove his oxen.

Usage

"Elisha of Abel-meholah was plowing when Elijah found him."

"The Midianites fled to the border of Abel-meholah and Tabbath."

"Abel-meholah lay in the fruitful plain of the Jordan valley."
